title: POC SLO Prioritization & Measurement Plan (TTFT vs TPOT)
summary: Initial scoping to pick primary latency vs throughput SLOs for a Calyx Retail inference POC. Discussed TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (total-prompt-throughput) tradeoffs, sample p95/p99 targets, workload sizing (concurrency, qps, token distributions), and an agreed measurement plan including warm/cold cache runs and synthetic vs production traffic windows. Action: Redwood to share harness + runbook; Calyx to provide traffic CSV and test dataset. Target pilot run week-of Jan 26.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48m
Recording ID: ff-20260110-8a3f-poz
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Alex (Redwood SE), Priya (Calyx Head of ML), Tom (Calyx Infra), Samantha (Calyx Product), Jorge (Calyx SRE)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick agenda — align on success criteria for the POC, pick which SLOs we prioritize (TTFT or TPOT), agree measurement plan and timeline.
00:18 Priya: Yep, thanks. We're primarily focused on chat and product recommendation inference. We have a bursty e-commerce pattern — spikes around promotions.
00:31 Alex: Cool. Quick clarifying point on terminology — when I say TTFT I'm referring to time to first token observer at the API front-door, so that includes request routing, model startup if cold, and first-token generation, roughly e2e. TPOT here we're using total prompt throughput — aggregate tokens/sec across the pool for sustained throughput.
00:52 Tom: Right, we care about both. Customer-facing latency is more TTFT, but cost and capacity planning leans on TPOT.
01:10 Samantha: For success criteria we want: 1) p95 conversational TTFT below ~250ms for short prompts, 2) p99 under 500ms, and 3) sustained TPOT to handle peak promo load with <=5% tail breaches. But these are initial, open to your guidance.
01:34 Alex: That's a reasonable starting point. For this POC we usually split acceptance into two classes: latency-first workloads (prioritize TTFT) and throughput-first (TPOT). We map your traffic profile and pick a primary objective. If product is heavily interactive UX, TTFT gets higher weight.
01:52 Priya: Our checkout assistant is interactive, so TTFT matters there. Recommendation batch inference can be TPOT-centric.
02:05 Maya: Let's scope the POC to cover both: conversational flow (TTFT-focused, small prompt sizes ~20-60 tokens) and batch recs (TPOT-focused, average prompt 200 tokens). We can run separate benchmark suites and A/B the model variants.
02:28 Jorge: A few infra constraints — we need VPC private deployment for PCI scope later, but for POC hosted is ok. We'll need a list of required audit fields and a security questionnaire.
02:40 Maya: We'll send the security docs. For measurement, key signals: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT aggregate tokens/sec, model GPU util, queue latency, 95/99 queue depth, and end-to-end client observed latency.
03:03 Alex: Methodology proposal: three-run experiment per scenario: cold-start run (no KV priming, restart model), warm run after a 10-minute priming ramp, and steady-state sustained run at target concurrency for 10 minutes. Collect token-level timestamps, start/end times, and per-request metadata (prompt length, model variant, route).
03:26 Tom: How do you simulate our burst patterns? We have promo spikes up to 8x baseline QPS over 5-10 minutes.
03:38 Alex: We'll provide a load generator config where you can inject a traffic CSV so the generator replays real inter-arrival times. That addresses burstiness. Also we'll run a sustained step test to measure TPOT at different concurrency levels to find knee points.
03:59 Priya: About SLO numbers — Samantha suggested p95 TTFT <= 250ms. Is that realistic for a medium-sized open model?
04:12 Maya: Depends on model and infra. For a 7B-ish quantized model on dedicated GPUs, p95 TTFT under 200-300ms for short prompts is possible with prefix caching and optimized kernel selection. p99 will be higher; 400-600ms range is common without more parallelism or scaling.
04:33 Samantha: What's the difference practically between TTFT and TPOT in measurement? I get the concept but need clarity for product KPI mapping.
04:45 Alex: TTFT maps to user-noticeable latency — first token. TPOT maps to how many tokens you can produce per second given your reserved capacity — it impacts cost and concurrency planning. For example, you could optimize for TTFT by keeping more warm replicas idle, which raises cost but reduces first-token latency; optimizing TPOT leans on batching and sustained utilization to lower per-token cost.
05:12 Jorge: We also need to capture cold vs warm KV cache behavior — first request after a redeploy is often a big outlier. How do you account for that in SLOs?
05:25 Alex: Good point. Our measurement plan separates cold start windows and we explicitly exclude cold restart windows from steady-state SLO calculation, but we report them. For contractual SLAs we recommend focusing on steady-state SLOs and describing expected cold-start windows and mitigations (keep-alives, pinned warm pools).
05:46 Priya: For POC acceptance, could we do: PASS if steady-state TTFT p95 <= 250ms and steady-state TPOT (aggregate tokens/sec) meets 80% of target throughput in the promo profile?
06:00 Maya: Yep, that maps well. Let's define the exact numbers: we need Calyx's token target. Tom, can you share QPS and average token lengths per route?
06:12 Tom: I can share a CSV: baseline QPS 120, peak 960 during promos (8x), average session prompt 40 tokens for chat, batch prompt 220 tokens, concurrency distribution attached. We'll upload to the shared drive.
06:28 Alex: With that profile, we recommend target TPOT for the chat route around 1200-1800 tokens/sec sustained across the reserved pool during promo peaks, but that'll depend on model choice and quantization. We'll size a dedicated pool with autoscale headroom for burst.
06:45 Samantha: How many clients/threads should we run from our side when doing the test?
06:50 Alex: We'll provide a recommended harness. Typically we run multiple injectors across machines to avoid client bottlenecks; use the replay CSV so traffic shape is preserved. We'll also collect client-side timestamps and Redwood-side timestamps to compute network vs model latency.
07:12 Maya: On acceptance criteria doc — we'll produce a small matrix: per-route SLOs, measurement windows, and the pass/fail thresholds. We'll include notes for observability: token-level logs, per-token timing, GPU util traces, and error rates.
07:33 Priya: On statistical significance — what's your suggested sample sizes?
07:39 Alex: For tail estimates (p99) we want thousands of samples in steady state; 10k+ requests per run is ideal. We'll run 3 repeats and report median/iqr across runs. For burst behavior we capture entire burst window; for promo we want to see at least 2 promo cycles if possible.
07:59 Jorge: Any special considerations for batching and caching interactions? e.g., batching can increase TPOT but spike first-token latency.
08:09 Alex: Exactly. We will run two config axes: low-latency config (minimal batching, more replicas) and high-throughput config (aggressive batching, higher utilization). We'll log batch sizes, queuing times, and include a configuration mapping file in the deliverable.
08:30 Samantha: Can you include approximate cost delta between configs? Our finance partner needs at least ballpark numbers.
08:36 Maya: We'll include relative unit-cost estimates (tokens/unit) for each config and SLO tier — not an invoice but an internal estimate for decisioning.
08:47 Priya: Timeline? When can we run the POC?
08:51 Maya: Proposed timeline: this week share harness + runbook, by Jan 20 we receive traffic CSV & dataset, run dry runs week of Jan 20, full pilot runs week of Jan 26, results + recommendations by Feb 2. Is that acceptable?
09:08 Tom: Yes, that works, provided we get the runbook and access details. We'll need a test VPC endpoint and API keys for the hosted interface.
09:19 Alex: We'll share ephemeral keys and guidance; for private deployments we can set up a staging VPC later.
09:28 Samantha: What about measurement artifacts — will you share raw logs?
09:31 Maya: We'll share sanitized logs, CSV summaries, and the bench harness config. Raw GPU traces can be shared on request but may require an NDA addendum.
09:43 Priya: Any red flags? We have strict compliance — SOC2 + PCI roadmap. Does hosting the POC data expose us?
09:53 Maya: For the hosted POC we recommend redacting PII in test dataset and use synthetic IDs. For deeper compliance testing we'll move to a private deployment. We'll also provide KMS/Encryption docs.
10:08 Jorge: For acceptance criteria: can you put in the doc how you calculate SLO breaches (sliding window vs global)? We have a monitoring policy that uses a 5-minute sliding window.
10:20 Alex: We'll include both 5-min sliding window breaches and run-level aggregated percentages. For contractual SLOs, we usually specify run-level percentages with a 30-day rolling window, but for POC a 5-min window and run-level aggregation is fine.
10:36 Priya: A few concrete numbers to record here: TTFT steady-state target p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 500ms for chat route (20-60 tokens). TPOT target: sustain >= 1,200 tokens/sec for chat during promo with <=5% p95 breaches. For batch recs: TPOT target sustain >= 1,800 tokens/sec (longer prompts), with p95 TTFT less critical.
11:05 Maya: I'll note that TTFT numbers assume quantized model and tuned kernels; if you pick a larger model we'll need to set different expectations.
11:15 Tom: Understood. We'll try with two model sizes — M1 (7B quantized) and M2 (13B int8) as variants.
11:26 Alex: Good plan. For measurement we'll tag each request with model_variant and record per-token GPU timing so we can do per-variant comparison.
11:40 Samantha: For delivery, what's the format of the final report?
11:45 Maya: PDF + spreadsheet with raw metrics + bench harness repo link + runbook. We'll include a one-page executive summary and a technical appendix.
11:54 Priya: Ok. Anything else on scope?
12:00 Maya: Quick recap — Redwood to share harness, runbook, and estimated cost delta. Calyx to share traffic CSV, sample prompts/dataset, and confirm models to test. Pilot dry-run week of Jan 20, full pilot week of Jan 26, final report Feb 2.
12:16 Jorge: Sounds good.
12:19 Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the doc and action items.
12:27 End of recording.
